task: Test the thesis: GLP-1 drug adoption is a lasting volume headwind for Mondelez

merged.claim: Gallup (survey May 28–June 5, 2026): 11% of US adults currently taking GLP-1 medications for weight loss, versus 3% in 2024.

variants.A: Gallup found 11% of U.S. adults currently taking GLP-1 medications for weight loss (survey as of 2026-06-05, revised 2026-09-08), versus 3% in its 2024 comparison.
variants.B: Gallup's May 28–June 5, 2026 survey found 11% of US adults currently taking GLP-1 medications for weight loss, versus 3% in 2024.
variants.F: Gallup reports 11% of U.S. adults were currently using GLP-1 medications for weight loss as of its May 28–June 5, 2026 survey, versus 3% in 2024 (self-reported weight-loss use; page revised September 8, 2026).

merged.claim: Gallup: 15% of US adults have ever used a GLP-1 in 2026, up from 6% in 2024.

variants.E: Gallup found 15% of US adults have ever used a GLP-1 in 2026, up from 6% in 2024 (as of July 2026).

merged.claim: KFF: 12% of US adults currently taking a GLP-1 in late 2025 (6% in May 2024; 12% again March 2026); Gallup weight-loss use 11% in June 2026 vs 3% in 2024 and 8% in 2025, implying ~29-32 million US users.

variants.D: KFF Health Tracking Poll: 12% of US adults were currently taking a GLP-1 for any reason in late 2025, double the 6% in May 2024, and 12% again in March 2026; Gallup put weight-loss-specific use at 11% in June 2026, up from 3% in 2024 and 8% in 2025, implying roughly 29-32 million current US users.

variants.D: US households with at least one GLP-1 user: Circana 23% (November 2025), Numerator 22% (August 2026), PwC 21% (May 2026).

variants.D: Per Lindt & Sprüngli citing Circana, 15% of US households had GLP-1 members as of February 2026 yet accounted for 17.5% of chocolate sales; US GLP-1 users spent almost 17% more on premium chocolate in 2025 vs a 6.5% increase among non-users.

merged.claim: Circana: 37% of US households have ever used a GLP-1.

variants.E: Circana reports 37% of US households have ever used a GLP-1.

variants.C: PwC reported that 21% of U.S. households included a current GLP-1 user as of May 2026, up from 9% in January 2025.

variants.C: PwC found 54% of surveyed GLP-1 users had been on the drugs for more than a year, 61% said they were buying fewer sweet treats and 56% fewer salty snacks (report dated 2026-06-22).

merged.claim: JMR study (~150,000 Numerator households): within six months of GLP-1 adoption, grocery spending -5.3% (higher-income -8.2%), limited-service restaurants -8.0%, savory snacks -10.1%.

variants.D: Journal of Marketing Research study (Hristakeva/Liaukonyte/Feler, ~150,000 Numerator households): within six months of GLP-1 adoption, households cut grocery spending 5.3% (higher-income 8.2%), limited-service restaurant spending fell 8.0%, and savory snacks fell 10.1%.

variants.D: Same study, category detail: chips and savory snacks -11.5%, sweet bakery -8.5%, frozen sides -7.5%, cheese -7.2%, cookies -7.0%, soft drinks -6.8%, candy and chocolate -3.5%, alcohol -1.4%; cookies, sweet bakery and chocolate are Mondelez categories.

merged.claim: Transaction study (July 2022–Sept 2024): within six months of adoption, spending fell 6.5% on cookies, 8.8% on sweet bakery and 10.1% on chips/savory snacks (category spending, not Mondelez unit volume).

merged.claim: Grocery spending remained below baseline in months 7-12 of GLP-1 use / food-demand adjustments persisted through the first year, though attenuated.

variants.F: In the same transaction study, grocery spending remained below baseline during months seven through twelve of GLP-1 use, although the effect attenuated.
variants.B: The Cornell/Numerator study's June 2026 journal publication reports that food-demand adjustments persisted through the first year of GLP-1 medication use, although they attenuated after six months.

merged.claim: Grocery-spending reduction eased from 5.3% (months 1-6) to ~4% (months 7-12), and the weight-loss-user effect in months 7-12 was statistically indistinguishable from zero.

variants.C: In transaction data, the GLP-1 grocery-spending reduction eased from 5.3% in months 1-6 to about 4% in months 7-12, and the weight-loss-user effect in months 7-12 was statistically indistinguishable from zero.

merged.claim: Cornell summary: lower spending persisted at least a year among continuing GLP-1 households but effects shrank; post-discontinuation effects hard to distinguish from pre-adoption; about one-third stopped during study.

variants.C: Cornell's summary of the transaction research reports lower spending persisted at least a year among households that continued GLP-1 use, but effects became smaller over time; effects after discontinuation were hard to distinguish from pre-adoption spending, and about one-third of users stopped during the study (2025-12-18).

variants.E: The Cornell/Numerator study found savory snack spending fell about 10% among GLP-1 households, with similar pullbacks in sweets, baked goods and cookies; the lower spending lasted at least a year among continuing users, though it moderated.

merged.claim: Study: household spending moved back toward baseline after GLP-1 discontinuation, with uncertainty whether recovery was complete.

variants.F: In the July 2022–September 2024 purchasing study, household spending moved back toward baseline after GLP-1 discontinuation, with uncertainty about whether recovery was complete.

merged.claim: Cornell/Numerator: candy-and-chocolate spending 11.4% above baseline after GLP-1 discontinuation; grocery spending generally reverted toward pre-adoption levels.

variants.B: In the Cornell/Numerator panel, candy-and-chocolate spending was 11.4% above baseline after GLP-1 discontinuation, and grocery spending generally reverted toward pre-adoption levels after stopping.

merged.claim: Study limitation: cannot separate drug effects from concurrent lifestyle changes or selection; measures (household spending, total grocery item counts) don't directly measure Mondelez product weight or units.

variants.F: The purchasing study (July 2022–September 2024 data) could not separate drug effects from concurrent lifestyle changes or unobserved selection, and its measures (household spending and total grocery item counts) do not directly measure Mondelez branded product weight or units.

variants.B: The Cornell/Numerator study describes its evidence as descriptive: treatment was not randomly assigned, unobserved health motivations could influence purchases, and purchases are not actual consumption.
